opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's going to take longer than a lot of people expect, and it's going to happen more gradually than the hype suggests.

There's this thing I call the "100,000-year data gap." Language models were trained on an enormous amount of text, roughly what it would take a human about 100,000 years to read. For robotics we have nothing close to that. We don't have a huge corpus of examples of robots folding laundry, loading dishwashers, or picking up a sock from under a couch. So the idea that we'll just scale up the same recipe and get a general-purpose household robot next year is, I think, overly optimistic.

That doesn't mean I'm a pessimist. I think the path to usefulness runs through specific, well-defined tasks where robots can be reliable, and through combining approaches. We shouldn't throw out good old-fashioned engineering: physics, geometry, analytic models of grasping. If we pair that with learning, we can bootstrap. You deploy robots on tasks they can already do reasonably well, they collect data as they work, and that data improves them. That's the data flywheel, and I think it's much more promising than hoping simulation or teleoperation alone will close the gap.

For the home specifically, I'd look for a few things. First, decluttering. Picking up objects off the floor and putting them where they belong sounds mundane, but it's something people genuinely want, and it's a tractable manipulation problem. Second, laundry. We've done work on folding, and it's very hard because fabric is deformable and has essentially infinite configurations, but progress is real. Third, tasks for the elderly and people with disabilities, where even modest help matters a great deal.

The key barrier to adoption isn't just capability, it's reliability and cost. A robot that succeeds 80 percent of the time is impressive in a lab and frustrating in your kitchen. People will tolerate a Roomba that gets stuck now and then because it's cheap and the stakes are low. A robot handling your grandmother's china has to clear a much higher bar.

So my vision is incremental. Robots will earn their place in homes one task at a time, starting with low-stakes, high-frequency chores, getting better as they gather real-world experience. I'd rather set expectations honestly, because overpromising tends to produce a backlash that hurts the field. The progress is exciting. It just won't look like Rosie from *The Jetsons* walking in the door all at once.

r001.rationale: The response mentions decluttering and laundry but does not compare cleanup with cooking or express a preference between them.

r002.rationale: It identifies cost as a barrier but does not propose economies of scale as a way to make household robots affordable.

r003.rationale: It says robots can collect data while doing tasks and that this data improves them over time.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I want to be careful here, because I've been in robotics for almost 40 years and I've watched people predict the home robot was right around the corner for that entire time. So let me start with a little humility.

The core problem is that homes are the hardest environment we could possibly pick. A factory is structured. The parts arrive in the same place, under the same lighting, and the robot does the same motion a million times. Your kitchen is the opposite. Every home is different, the objects are different, they get moved around, there's clutter, there are kids and pets and that one drawer that sticks. And the thing people underestimate is how hard manipulation still is. Grasping a wine glass, folding a towel, picking a sock out of a pile: these are things a two-year-old can do and robots still struggle with reliably. I call this Moravec's paradox in action. The things that are hard for humans, like chess or calculus, turned out to be easy for computers, and the things that are effortless for us turned out to be incredibly hard.

So how does it become useful enough? I think about it in a few ways.

First, we have to lower the bar on what "useful" means. The fantasy is Rosie from the Jetsons, a general-purpose humanoid that does everything. I think that's the wrong target for now. The Roomba is actually the most successful home robot in history, and it does exactly one thing, imperfectly, in a way that's good enough. I expect the next wave looks more like that: narrow, specific tasks where the robot can fail gracefully. Clearing a table, loading a dishwasher, tidying up objects off the floor. Tasks where if it drops something, nobody gets hurt.

Second, reliability matters more than capability. In a lab demo, 80 percent success looks amazing. In your home, 80 percent means it breaks a glass every fifth time, and you'll unplug it within a week. We need something like 99 percent plus, and getting that last bit is enormously harder than getting the first 80. This is where I'm a bit skeptical of some of the current hype around end-to-end learning. The data is just not there yet. We have trillions of words on the internet to train language models. We do not have anything like that for robot manipulation, because nobody has been recording what their hands do all day.

Third, and this is something I've been pushing for a long time, I don't think full autonomy is the right frame. I think of it as a spectrum with humans in the loop. A robot in the home that can call out to a remote human when it gets confused, even briefly, suddenly becomes much more viable. The robot handles the routine 95 percent and a person resolves the edge cases, and every one of those interventions becomes training data that makes the system better. That's a flywheel that could actually work, and it's one that companies are starting to pursue.

And then there's cost and safety. You need something that costs on the order of a car, not a house, and that can operate around a toddler without anyone worrying. Those are solvable but they're not solved.

So my honest view is: I'm very optimistic over a 10 to 20 year horizon and quite cautious over a 2 to 3 year one. The progress in the last few years is real. Vision and language models have given robots a kind of common sense they never had before, so a robot can now understand "put the dishes away" as a concept. But understanding the sentence and actually getting the plates into the cupboard without chipping them are very different problems, and the second one is still where most of the difficulty lives.

r001.rationale: It lists clearing tables, loading dishwashers, and tidying as possible narrow tasks, but does not express a preference for cleanup over cooking.

r002.rationale: It says a robot should cost about as much as a car, but does not propose economies of scale as a way to make it affordable.

r003.rationale: It says human interventions when a robot is confused become training data that improves the system, describing a feedback loop during use.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to start with a fairly narrow task and do it reliably. We tend to imagine a household robot as something that can cook dinner, fold the laundry, clear the table, and put everything away. But each of those involves an enormous variety of objects and situations. Even picking up a shirt is difficult, because its shape changes as you touch it.

So I’d expect adoption to be gradual. A robot that takes care of one chore, with very little setup or supervision, can be useful even if it doesn’t look anything like a person. The question is whether it actually saves you effort. If you have to rescue it every few minutes, the benefit disappears.

And there may be an intermediate stage where robots can ask for help when they encounter something unfamiliar. They don’t necessarily have to handle every possible situation independently. But they do need to recognize their limits and fail safely. To me, that’s a more plausible path into the home: useful capabilities that gradually expand as reliability improves.

r001.rationale: The response lists cooking and clearing the table as examples of difficult chores, but it does not state a preference for cleanup over cooking.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention economies of scale or affordability.

r003.rationale: The response discusses reliability improving over time, but does not identify data collected during deployment as the means of improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to start with a very limited set of tasks and do those reliably. We tend to imagine a robot that can walk into any home and do everything a person does. But even something like clearing a dinner table involves an enormous variety of objects and situations. There’s a glass with some water left in it, a plate with food on it, a napkin partly underneath something else. What looks routine to us is quite challenging for a robot.

So I imagine adoption happening gradually, around particular jobs that people really want help with. And the important measure won’t just be whether the robot can demonstrate the task. It’ll be how often you have to intervene. If you’re constantly rescuing it, you haven’t really saved any time.

There may also be a useful role for remote human assistance when the robot gets stuck. It doesn’t necessarily need to solve every unusual situation autonomously on day one. But the whole system has to be safe, affordable, and useful enough that people actually want it in their homes.
